title: Essentials
about: A 250-hour track through the same reading list. Thirteen modules of roughly 12 to 25 hours each. In each module you read short, specific passages from the key works. You then survey the module's other works by reading their descriptions, about a minute each, so every one of the 571 entries is covered at least at the level of its main idea. Hour figures are rough estimates for the assigned passages.

modules.title: How to Read and Argue
modules.intro: The classical tools for reading and arguing: definition, the syllogism, the common fallacies, the parts of a speech, and the geometric proof. These are enough to follow the arguments in every later module.
takeaways: Classification comes before argument. Genus, species, and difference are the basis of a definition.
A syllogism is valid because of its form, whatever its content. Fallacies are arguments that only look valid.
Rhetoric has five parts: invention, arrangement, style, memory, and delivery. Euclid's method of building from axioms became the model of certain knowledge.
modules.check: Take one argument you have heard this week. Put it in syllogistic form and name any fallacy it commits.

readings.read: The whole text; it is short. Learn the five predicables.
Chapters 1-5, ending with the account of substance.
Prior Analytics I.1-7 (the syllogism) and Sophistical Refutations 4-5 (the thirteen fallacies).
Book I.2-4 (the five canons and the parts of a speech) and Book III.16-24 (the art of memory).
Book I: definitions, postulates, common notions, then propositions 1-5 and 47 (the Pythagorean theorem).

modules.title: Homer and the Gods
modules.intro: The Iliad and the Odyssey are the most frequently referenced works in the Western sections of the list. This module reads the books that carry each poem's plot and turning points, plus Hesiod's account of the gods and the earliest Greek lyric.
takeaways: The Iliad is about the anger of Achilles, and about honor, mortality, and recognizing a shared humanity in an enemy (Priam and Achilles in Book 24).
The Odyssey is about cunning, homecoming, and xenia, the obligations between guest and host.
Hesiod gives the family tree of the gods and a moral picture of justice and labor.
modules.check: What does Achilles learn between Book 9 and Book 24?

readings.read: Theogony 1-210 (creation and Kronos) and Works and Days 1-201 (Prometheus, Pandora, the five ages).
Fragments 1, 16, and 31.

modules.title: Tragedy, History, and the City
modules.intro: Athens in the fifth century BC produced tragedy, comedy, and history writing within a few decades. Read two tragedians, one comedy, and the founding passages of the two founding historians.
takeaways: Tragedy stages conflicts that have no clean resolution: vengeance against justice, family against the law of the city.
Herodotus explains events through custom and fortune. Thucydides explains them through power, fear, and interest.
The Melian dialogue is the classic statement of 'the strong do what they can and the weak suffer what they must'.
modules.check: Compare Antigone and Creon with the Athenians and Melians. Who appeals to what law?

readings.read: Agamemnon and The Eumenides, the first and last plays of the trilogy.
Oedipus the King and Antigone.
The Bacchae.
The Clouds, a comic portrait of Socrates.
The preface and I.1-45 (Croesus and Solon); VII.201-239 (Thermopylae).
I.20-23 (method); II.35-54 (Funeral Oration and plague); III.82-83 (civil strife at Corcyra); V.84-116 (the Melian dialogue).

modules.title: Plato and Aristotle
modules.intro: The two philosophers whose questions set the agenda for the rest of the list: what justice is, what the soul is, what a good life is, and how we know anything. The passages below are the ones later writers quote most often.
takeaways: Plato: justice is an order in the soul and the city. True knowledge is of the Forms, and the Cave allegory shows the path from opinion to knowledge.
Aristotle: the good life is activity in accordance with virtue, virtue is a mean found by practical wisdom, and humans are political animals.
Heraclitus and Parmenides frame the question of change and permanence that both men answer.
modules.check: State in three sentences where Aristotle's ethics departs from Plato's Republic.

readings.read: The fragments of Heraclitus and of Parmenides only.

The Apology (not on the list) as a preface. Republic I-II (Thrasymachus and the Ring of Gyges), IV (the parts of the soul), VI.507-VII.521 (sun, line, cave), X.614-621 (Myth of Er). Symposium 201d-212c (Diotima). Phaedo 115-118 (the death of Socrates).
Nicomachean Ethics I, II, and X.6-8. Politics I.1-2. Poetics 6-14 (tragedy).

modules.title: Rome: Duty, Empire, and the Stoics
modules.intro: Rome took Greek culture and turned it toward law, duty, and empire, and it produced the Stoic writers still read as practical guides. This module gives you the founding myths, the national epic, and Stoicism in its own words.
takeaways: Roman virtue is duty to family, gods, and the state (pietas). Aeneas is its model, and Virgil shows what it costs.
The Stoics separate what is in our power (judgments, choices) from what is not (everything else).
The Epicureans (Lucretius) offer the rival cure: an atomic universe with no gods to fear and no death to suffer.
modules.check: Is Aeneas admirable in Book 4? Answer from Virgil's text, then from Epictetus.

readings.read: The Preface and I.1-16 (the founding); I.57-60 (Lucretia and the end of the kings).
The Life of Julius Caesar.
Books 1, 2, 4, 6, and 12.
I.1-158 (the invocation and 'nothing from nothing') and III.830-1094 ('death is nothing to us').
On Duties I.1-60 and On Friendship.
The whole text; it is a few pages.
Book I (creation, the flood, Apollo and Daphne) and Book X (Orpheus, Pygmalion).
The Agricola; it is short. Note Calgacus's speech (ch. 30).
The Enchiridion in full.
Books 2 and 4.
On the Shortness of Life.

modules.title: The Bible
modules.intro: Later European literature and philosophy constantly assume a knowledge of the Bible. These passages cover the narrative spine: creation, covenant, exodus, law, wisdom, prophecy, the life of Jesus, and the early church.
takeaways: One God who creates, makes covenants, and acts in history, unlike the gods of Homer and Hesiod.
Job and Ecclesiastes question the tradition from within: suffering that is not deserved, and the vanity of all things.
The Gospels and Paul recast the covenant around the death and resurrection of Jesus and salvation by grace.
modules.check: What question does Job ask, and does the voice from the whirlwind answer it?

Ecclesiastes in full; skim Proverbs 1-9.
Isaiah 1-6 and 40-55; Amos 5; Jeremiah 31.
Mark in full; Matthew 5-7 (the Sermon on the Mount); John 1 and 18-21.
Acts 1-2, 9, and 17.
Romans 1-8; 1 Corinthians 13 and 15.
Chapters 1, 4-5, and 21-22.

modules.title: Augustine and Late Antiquity
modules.intro: In the late Roman world, early Christian writers combined biblical faith with Greek philosophy. Augustine did so most influentially, and he had read Plotinus before his conversion. Through him the Middle Ages received both traditions.
takeaways: Christian doctrine (Incarnation, Trinity) was worked out in the vocabulary of Greek philosophy.
Augustine's Confessions invented the inward autobiography: memory, time, and a restless heart.
The City of God divides humanity by what it loves, the earthly city and the heavenly one, rather than by political allegiance.
modules.check: What did Augustine take from the Platonists, by his own account in Confessions VII, and what did he find missing?

readings.read: The whole text; it is short.
The first half of On the Incarnation.
Ennead I.6, On Beauty.
Books I-IV, VII-IX, and XI (on time).
Book XIV.28 (two loves, two cities) and Book XIX (peace and the ends of life).
The Prologue and chapters 4-7.
The Mystical Theology; it is a few pages.

modules.title: The Medieval World
modules.intro: Three strands in one module: the northern heroic poetry, the scholastic theology of the schools, and the courtly literature that ends in Dante and Chaucer. Boethius comes first because nearly every medieval writer knew him.
takeaways: The Germanic heroic ethic is loyalty, fame, and courage in the face of fate. Christian writers kept it and reinterpreted it.
Scholasticism reasons from authorities through objection and reply. Aquinas reconciles Aristotle with Christian faith.
Dante orders the whole cosmos morally. Chaucer puts the whole of English society on one pilgrimage.
modules.check: Compare Beowulf, Roland, and Gawain. What does each hero owe, and to whom?

readings.read: Books I-II (Philosophy's visit and the wheel of Fortune).
The whole poem, in a modern verse translation.
The Wanderer and The Dream of the Rood.
Voluspa and Havamal.
From the opening through Roland's death.
Proslogion 2-4, the ontological argument.
Summa Theologiae I q.2 a.3 (the five ways) and I-II qq.90-91 and 94 (law and natural law).

readings.match: 7:Anon. — Sir Gawain and the Green Knight
readings.read: The whole poem.
Inferno 1-5, 26, and 33-34; Purgatorio 1 and 30; Paradiso 33.
The General Prologue and the Pardoner's Tale.

modules.title: Judaism and Islam
modules.intro: Rabbinic law and ethics, the Qur'an and hadith, the medieval argument over philosophy and revelation, and Sufi poetry. The philosophers in this module passed Aristotle on to the Latin scholastics of Module 8.
takeaways: Rabbinic Judaism keeps both sides of an argument on record. The Torah is studied and interpreted in every generation.
The Qur'an stresses God's oneness (tawhid), prophecy, and judgment. Hadith and the life of the Prophet set the pattern of practice.
Al-Ghazali, Averroes, and Maimonides debate whether philosophy serves revelation or threatens it. The Sufi poets describe the way of love.
modules.check: Set Averroes' Decisive Treatise beside Aquinas on faith and reason. Where do they agree?

readings.read: The whole text.
Bava Metzia 59a-b (the oven of Akhnai) and Shabbat 31a (Hillel on the whole Torah).
The whole collection.

modules.title: India, China, and Japan
modules.intro: The Upanishads and the Gita, the Buddha's teaching and its development into Zen, and the Confucian and Daoist classics. The passages are short, and many are meant to be reread slowly.
takeaways: The Upanishads teach that atman (the self) is brahman (ultimate reality). The Gita teaches action without attachment to its results.
The Buddha teaches suffering, its cause, its end, and the path, and denies a permanent self (anatta). Mahayana and Zen develop this into emptiness and direct insight.
Confucius grounds order in ritual, family, and cultivated character. Laozi and Zhuangzi turn to spontaneity and the Way.
modules.check: Compare Krishna's advice to Arjuna with Epictetus's Enchiridion.

modules.title: Renaissance and the New Science
modules.intro: The recovery of ancient texts, a new political realism, the essay and the stage, and the attempt to rebuild knowledge on new foundations. The science of this period is covered here by survey. The philosophy is read directly.
takeaways: Renaissance humanism says human beings have no fixed place in creation and must make themselves (Pico).
Machiavelli and Hobbes ground politics in power and fear rather than in virtue or divine order.
Descartes starts philosophy over from the thinking self. Locke grounds government in consent and property.
modules.check: How would Hobbes answer Thrasymachus in Republic I?

modules.title: The Modern Mind
modules.intro: From the Enlightenment to the twentieth century: the limits of reason, revolution and its critics, history, the death of God, evolution, and the unconscious. The Forbidden Shelf is surveyed here too, as a record of the tradition's most radical critics.
takeaways: Hume doubts causation and the self. Kant answers that the mind structures experience, and grounds morality in duty.
Hegel and Marx read history as a development driven by conflict. Burke and Tocqueville warn about what revolutions and democracy can destroy.
Kierkegaard, Nietzsche, and Freud move the question of meaning into the individual, the will, and the unconscious.
modules.check: Nietzsche's madman announces the death of God. Name three thinkers in this module and how each responds, directly or not.

modules.title: The Modern Imagination
modules.intro: The novel, the lyric, and the drama of the last three centuries, read as answers to everything before them. Most readings are complete shorter works or pivotal chapters of long ones.
takeaways: Goethe and the Romantics make striving, nature, and feeling into sources of meaning.
The Russian novelists test modern ideas against faith, suffering, and death: the Underground Man, the Grand Inquisitor, Ivan Ilyich.
The modernists (Kafka, Conrad, Eliot, Camus) write about alienation, the absurd, and the search for order among fragments.
modules.check: Choose one work from this module and trace three of its sources back through earlier modules.
